description:
We are Byte Force, a team of six third-year Software Engineering students from Chernivtsi Polytechnic College, Ukraine.

Passionate about coding, innovation, and problem-solving, we're ready to turn bold ideas into real solutions. NASA Space Apps is our chance to challenge ourselves, explore new technologies, and create something meaningful.
summary:
Lunar Navigator is an interactive 3D tool for assessing potential research station sites near the Moon’s south pole. Users can explore one site or compare two over the same period.
The tool combines NASA’s LOLA elevation maps with Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons to estimate when each body lies above the local horizon formed by nearby terrain. Users can follow changes on a timeline and see the estimated duration for each body in hours and as a percentage of the selected period.
These estimates help researchers identify sites worth studying further for solar power generation and direct communication with Earth.
details:
Lunar Navigator is an interactive web application for assessing potential research station sites near the Moon’s south pole. Users can study a single location in detail or compare two candidate sites. In both modes, they choose the start and end of the analysis period in UTC and set the time step between calculations. For example, they can examine a 24-hour period at one-hour intervals or select a shorter step to follow changes in more detail.

For a single site, the analysis shows where the Sun and Earth appear in the local sky at each sampled time. A compass shows the direction to each body. The terrain profile shows how high the surrounding landscape rises in that direction. Users can switch the chart between two views: how high each body is above the horizontal plane, and how far it is above or below the modeled terrain skyline. They can select a moment on the timeline or play through the period to see how these values change.

In comparison mode, users can evaluate two sites over the same dates and at the same time step. Selecting a time on the shared timeline shows the results for both sites at that moment. The period summary answers a different question: over the full interval, how many hours was the Sun or Earth estimated to be above the local skyline at each site, and what percentage of the period does that represent? Users can then generate a report and export their results to document the comparison or share it with others.

The calculations combine Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL Horizons with an 80-metre elevation map derived from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). The application samples terrain up to 20 kilometres around each site to estimate the local skyline. Its distinctive feature is that users can connect a difference in the report to a specific place, direction, and time, then inspect it on the globe, terrain view, or chart. This supports early decisions about which sites deserve further study for solar power and direct communication with Earth. The estimates depend on the terrain coverage and time step. Predicting electrical output or radio link availability requires additional models.

The interface uses React and TypeScript, with Three.js and React Three Fiber for the 3D globe and terrain views. The C# backend uses ASP.NET Core to process analysis requests and retrieve data from Horizons. Python prepares the elevation data and generates the terrain assets. Users interact with the software through a web browser.
